scenarios.title: Building Your Study Plan
scenarios.situation: You have 6 weeks until your CISSP assessment. You work full-time and have 2 hours per evening plus weekends. You've tried studying before but kept losing momentum after week 2.
scenarios.prompt: What's the most effective study approach for sustained 6-week preparation?
choices: Follow the bootcamp's guided path in order: 2 hours daily mixing lessons, scenarios, and labs, with weekly review of weak areas and a full mock in week 5
Study 6 hours every Saturday and skip weekdays — cramming on weekends is more efficient
Read all lessons first (weeks 1-4), then do all scenarios (week 5), then labs (week 6)
Focus only on practice exams — studying content is less important than test familiarity
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Spaced, interleaved practice across 6 weeks builds durable knowledge. The guided path sequences foundations before advanced topics. Mixing lessons (input), scenarios (application), and labs (hands-on) every session engages all learning modes. Weekend-only cramming leads to burnout and poor retention. Reading everything before practicing means you forget early material.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the learning science says: spacing, interleaving, and active practice beat massed passive reading.
objectives: Design an effective multi-week study plan
Balance input, application, and hands-on practice
evidence: Spaced repetition improves long-term retention by 200%+ vs. massed practice (Cepeda et al.)

scenarios.title: Identifying Weak Areas
scenarios.situation: After 3 weeks of study, your scenario scores are: Networking 90%, Security 85%, Storage 60%, Troubleshooting 55%. The exam is in 3 weeks.
scenarios.prompt: How should you allocate your remaining study time?
choices: Shift 70% of study time to Storage and Troubleshooting (weakest areas) while maintaining Networking and Security with brief reviews
Continue studying all areas equally — balanced preparation is safest
Focus exclusively on Troubleshooting (lowest score) until it reaches 80%, then move on
Study only your strong areas to guarantee those points — weak areas are harder to improve
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Targeted remediation on weak areas yields the highest score improvement per hour. Your strong areas (90%, 85%) need only maintenance to prevent decay. Equal allocation wastes time on already-mastered content. Single-area focus risks neglecting Storage while over-investing in one domain.
scenarios.hint: Where is the most room for improvement? Which areas need maintenance vs. intensive work?
objectives: Analyze performance data to identify gaps
Prioritize study time for maximum score impact

scenarios.title: Exam Day Strategy
scenarios.situation: It's exam day. You have 90 minutes for 65 questions including performance-based simulations. You feel nervous.
scenarios.prompt: What's the best time management strategy?
choices: Quick first pass: answer confident questions immediately, flag uncertain ones, do performance-based last, then return to flagged items with remaining time
Answer every question in order, spending as much time as needed to be certain before moving on
Start with performance-based questions while your mind is fresh, then do multiple choice
Rush through all questions in 45 minutes, then use remaining time to double-check everything
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The two-pass method ensures you bank all confident points first, then allocate remaining time to harder questions. Performance-based questions are time-intensive — doing them last prevents getting stuck early. Answering in strict order risks running out of time on difficult items while easy points remain unclaimed.
scenarios.hint: Think about maximizing points per minute. Which questions give the best return on time invested?
objectives: Prioritize questions by confidence and time cost
evidence: 90 minutes | 65 questions | Mix of MCQ and performance-based

scenarios.title: When Reading Isn't Enough
scenarios.situation: You've read all the lessons twice and score 95% on knowledge checks, but only 60% on scenario questions and struggle with labs.
scenarios.prompt: What's the gap and how do you fix it?
choices: Knowledge without application: shift to scenarios and labs — narrate your reasoning aloud, redo failed labs until fluent, and practice explaining the 'why' behind each answer
Read the lessons a third time more carefully — you must have missed details
The scenarios are poorly written — focus on memorizing more facts instead
Take a break from studying — you're overthinking the practical questions
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. High knowledge-check scores with low scenario scores indicate a transfer gap — you know facts but can't apply them. Scenarios require connecting concepts to situations. Labs require procedural fluency. The fix is deliberate application practice: think aloud through scenarios, repeat labs until commands are automatic, and always ask 'why is this the best answer?' not just 'what is the answer?'
scenarios.hint: What's different between a knowledge check (recall) and a scenario (application)? Which skill needs practice?
objectives: Apply deliberate practice to build transfer

scenarios.title: Doing the ALE math
scenarios.situation: A risk analyst reports: an asset valued at $500,000, an exposure factor of 40% for a flood scenario, and an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.5.
scenarios.prompt: What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
scenarios.why: Single loss expectancy SLE = asset value x exposure factor = $500,000 x 0.40 = $200,000. ALE = SLE x ARO = $200,000 x 0.5 = $100,000. ALE lets you compare the cost of a control against the loss it prevents.
scenarios.hint: Compute SLE first: what is one flood's loss?

scenarios.title: The unpatchable legacy system
scenarios.situation: A legacy control system cannot be patched, and replacing it costs far more than the expected loss. The residual risk sits above the company's risk appetite, but cyber-insurance is available.
scenarios.prompt: Which risk treatment fits best?
choices: Transfer — buy insurance and formally document the accepted residual risk
Avoid — shut the system down regardless of business impact
Ignore — appetite is just a guideline
Mitigate — apply the same patch anyway
scenarios.why: The four treatments are avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept. When mitigation is not cost-effective and avoidance kills the business, transferring financial impact via insurance — with documented acceptance of what remains — is the defensible choice.
scenarios.hint: Which option pays someone else to carry the financial impact?

scenarios.title: No reliable numbers
scenarios.situation: You must assess the risk of a novel AI feature, but there is no historical loss data and the impact ranges are pure guesses.
scenarios.prompt: Which assessment approach is appropriate?
choices: Qualitative — use structured expert judgment (scenarios, Delphi) with defined scales
Quantitative — invent precise numbers to look rigorous
Skip the assessment until data exists
Copy a competitor's numbers
scenarios.why: Quantitative analysis needs credible numbers; fabricating them produces false precision. Qualitative methods use calibrated scales (e.g., 1–5 likelihood/impact) and expert consensus — honest about uncertainty and still decision-useful.
scenarios.hint: What do you use when the numbers would be guesses?

scenarios.title: Policy versus guideline
scenarios.situation: A new administrator asks which document wins when the acceptable-use policy and a best-practice guideline disagree.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct hierarchy?
choices: Policy > standard > procedure > guideline — the mandatory policy prevails
Guideline > policy — best practice always wins
Whichever was written most recently
They are all equal
scenarios.why: Policies are mandatory high-level directives from management; standards define mandatory specifics; procedures give step-by-step instructions; guidelines are recommended (not mandatory) advice. Higher authority and mandatory force win.
scenarios.hint: Which document is both mandatory and highest-level?

scenarios.title: Labeling the crown jewels
scenarios.situation: The company holds customer Social Security numbers, internal memos, and published marketing copy. A classification scheme is being rolled out.
scenarios.prompt: How should the SSNs be classified?
choices: Restricted (or confidential/top tier) — strictest handling, encryption, and access controls
Public — like the marketing copy
Internal — same as the memos
Unclassified — labels slow people down
scenarios.why: Classification matches handling to harm: SSNs enable identity theft, so they get the highest tier with encryption, least-privilege access, and retention limits. Marketing copy is public; memos are internal. One flat label either overprotects trivia or underprotects PII.
scenarios.hint: What is the harm if this data becomes public?

scenarios.title: Who classifies the data?
scenarios.situation: IT argues the security team should classify all company data; the business units say it is their call.
scenarios.prompt: Who is right?
choices: The data owner (business) classifies — they understand the data's value; custodians (IT) implement the controls
The security team classifies everything alone
Nobody — classification is optional
The auditors classify during audits
scenarios.why: Ownership follows business accountability: the data owner decides classification based on value and sensitivity, while custodians maintain the systems and apply the controls. Security advises and verifies; it does not own the business's data.
scenarios.hint: Who understands the data's value best?

scenarios.title: Retiring the drives
scenarios.situation: Decommissioned servers held restricted data. The retention schedule says financial records must be kept seven years; the servers are being scrapped now.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct disposition?
choices: Sanitize per classification (cryptographic erase or destruction) and retain required records per the schedule
Sell the servers as-is to recover value
Format the drives and donate them
Keep everything forever to be safe
scenarios.why: End-of-life media with restricted data needs sanitization matched to classification — destruction or crypto-erase — with certificates for audit. Retention schedules govern records, not hardware: required records move to archival storage, not the scrap heap.
scenarios.hint: What does the retention schedule say — and what does the scrapyard get?

scenarios.title: The litigation letter
scenarios.situation: Legal notifies you of impending litigation involving email from the past three years. The normal retention policy would delete mail older than one year next week.
scenarios.prompt: What takes precedence?
choices: The legal hold — suspend routine deletion for the affected data immediately
The retention policy — it is already approved
Delete faster before the hold is formalized
Ask IT to decide
scenarios.why: A legal hold overrides retention schedules: destroying potentially relevant data after notice is spoliation, with severe penalties. Holds must be communicated, scoped, and enforced technically — then lifted formally when released.
scenarios.hint: Which obligation wins when they conflict?

scenarios.title: Reading up
scenarios.situation: A user cleared to Secret tries to open a document marked Top Secret on a system enforcing Bell-LaPadula.
scenarios.prompt: What happens, and why?
choices: Access is denied — Bell-LaPadula enforces 'no read up' to protect confidentiality
Access is granted — clearance is close enough
Access is granted but logged
The document is downgraded automatically
scenarios.why: Bell-LaPadula is the confidentiality model: the simple security property ('no read up') stops information flowing to lower clearances, and the *-property ('no write down') stops leaks downward. Reading up would violate the model's core guarantee.
scenarios.hint: In a confidentiality model, can a subject read above its clearance?

scenarios.title: Protecting the ledger
scenarios.situation: A bank needs a formal model to guarantee that low-integrity data can never corrupt high-integrity financial records.
scenarios.prompt: Which model fits?
choices: Biba — the integrity model ('no write up, no read down' in its strict form)
Bell-LaPadula — the confidentiality model
Clark-Wilson — useful, but the question asks for the classic integrity model
Brewer-Nash — the conflict-of-interest model
scenarios.why: Biba is the classic integrity counterpart to Bell-LaPadula: it prevents low-integrity subjects from writing to high-integrity objects. (Clark-Wilson also addresses integrity via transactions, but Biba is the canonical lattice integrity model.)
scenarios.hint: Which model is about integrity rather than secrecy?

scenarios.title: Encrypting the archive
scenarios.situation: You must encrypt 10 TB of archival data at rest. Performance matters; key exchange happens rarely and separately.
scenarios.prompt: Which cryptographic approach fits?
choices: Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) for the bulk data — fast; use asymmetric only for key exchange
Asymmetric encryption for all 10 TB
Hashing the archive instead of encrypting
Base64 encoding
scenarios.why: Symmetric ciphers like AES are orders of magnitude faster for bulk data; asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECC) is used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk encryption. Hashing is one-way and cannot be decrypted; Base64 is encoding, not encryption.
scenarios.hint: Which is faster for gigabytes — symmetric or asymmetric?

scenarios.title: The key in the repo
scenarios.situation: A developer committed a cloud API key to a public Git repository 'temporarily' six months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response?
choices: Treat the key as compromised: revoke and rotate it, scan for abuse, and move secrets to a vault/KMS
Delete the commit and assume safety
Leave it — it still works
Change the repo to private and move on
scenarios.why: Secrets in version control are compromised the moment they are pushed — history preserves them and scrapers harvest public repos in minutes. Revoke, rotate, audit for misuse, and enforce vault-based secret management with pre-commit scanning.
scenarios.hint: Who else can read that repository's history?

scenarios.title: Placing the web server
scenarios.situation: A new public-facing web portal must be deployed. The internal network holds regulated customer data.
scenarios.prompt: Where does the portal belong?
choices: In a DMZ — screened by firewalls on both the internet and internal sides
Directly on the internal LAN for easy management
On the public internet with no firewall
On the CEO's laptop
scenarios.why: A DMZ (screened subnet) hosts public services between two firewall boundaries: the outer firewall filters internet traffic, the inner firewall strictly limits DMZ-to-internal flows. A compromised portal then does not mean a compromised LAN.
scenarios.hint: Where do you put what the internet must touch?

scenarios.title: Connecting the branches
scenarios.situation: Five branch offices need always-on, site-to-site connectivity back to headquarters over the internet.
scenarios.prompt: Which VPN approach fits?
choices: IPsec site-to-site tunnels between the branch and HQ gateways
A TLS/SSL VPN client on every desktop
PPTP tunnels
No VPN — the internet is fine
scenarios.why: IPsec operates at the network layer and is the standard for gateway-to-gateway site connectivity, encrypting all inter-site traffic transparently. TLS VPNs suit remote users; PPTP is cryptographically broken and must not be used.
scenarios.hint: What connects networks to networks, rather than users to networks?

scenarios.title: Detect or prevent?
scenarios.situation: The SOC wants a control that automatically drops packets matching known attack signatures on the internet edge.
scenarios.prompt: Which control fits, and what is the trade-off?
choices: An IPS inline — it can block, but a false positive drops legitimate traffic
An IDS — it blocks traffic
A firewall — it detects intrusions
A honeypot — it blocks attacks
scenarios.why: An IDS only detects and alerts; an IPS sits inline and can drop malicious packets — at the cost that false positives become self-inflicted outages. Placement and tuning decide whether prevention helps or harms availability.
scenarios.hint: Which one can actually drop the packet?

scenarios.title: Stopping lateral movement
scenarios.situation: Ransomware spread across a flat corporate network in minutes, reaching every workstation from one phishing click.
scenarios.prompt: What architectural control would have contained it?
choices: Network segmentation (VLANs/firewalled zones) with least-privilege traffic rules between segments
A bigger flat network
More antivirus on each host alone
Faster workstations
scenarios.why: Flat networks let any compromise reach everything; segmentation breaks the network into zones so a breach is contained and east-west traffic is filtered. Host controls matter, but architecture determines blast radius.
scenarios.hint: What stops an attacker from walking sideways?

scenarios.title: Picking the second factor
scenarios.situation: A company is rolling out MFA. Options on the table: SMS codes, authenticator app codes, and hardware security keys.
scenarios.prompt: Which second factor is strongest, and why?
choices: Hardware security keys — phishing-resistant and immune to SIM-swapping, unlike SMS
SMS codes — everyone has a phone
Authenticator apps are weaker than SMS
MFA is unnecessary with long passwords
scenarios.why: Not all MFA is equal: SMS is vulnerable to SIM-swapping and interception, app codes resist that but remain phishable, while FIDO2 hardware keys bind authentication to the legitimate origin — the phishing-resistant choice.
scenarios.hint: What can be SIM-swapped?

scenarios.title: Federating the SaaS apps
scenarios.situation: Employees need single sign-on to a dozen SaaS applications using the corporate identity provider.
scenarios.prompt: Which standard is the enterprise federation choice?
choices: SAML — the established standard for web SSO federation between IdPs and service providers
Kerberos — for internet SaaS federation
Basic auth — simple and federated
Telnet
scenarios.why: SAML is the long-standing enterprise standard for browser-based SSO federation: the IdP authenticates once and asserts identity to each SaaS app. Kerberos suits on-prem Windows domains; OAuth/OIDC authorize and authenticate modern apps but SAML dominates enterprise SaaS federation.
scenarios.hint: What does the enterprise IdP speak to SaaS applications?

scenarios.title: The account that would not die
scenarios.situation: An audit finds accounts of employees who left 90+ days ago still active, one of which was used in an incident.
scenarios.prompt: What process failure allowed this, and what fixes it?
choices: Broken deprovisioning — tie account lifecycle to HR termination events with automated revocation
The accounts were too complex
Users need permanent accounts
Audits should be less frequent
scenarios.why: Joiner-mover-leaver processes must revoke access on termination automatically; manual, ticket-driven deprovisioning always lags. Orphaned accounts are a top attack path because nobody watches them.
scenarios.hint: What event should kill access automatically?

scenarios.title: One person, whole pipeline
scenarios.situation: A developer can write code, approve their own pull request, and deploy to production alone.
scenarios.prompt: Which principle is violated, and what is the fix?
choices: Separation of duties — split authorize, deploy, and audit across roles so no one person owns the full fraud chain
Least privilege — unrelated here
Defense in depth — unrelated here
Nothing — developers should be trusted
scenarios.why: Separation of duties ensures fraud or error needs collusion: the person who writes code cannot be the one who approves and ships it. Enforce via workflow roles plus technical controls, not policy alone.
scenarios.hint: What stops one person owning the entire fraud chain?

scenarios.title: Scan or pen test?
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants proof of whether an attacker could actually steal customer data through the new portal — not just a list of possible issues.
scenarios.prompt: Which assessment fits?
choices: A penetration test — it attempts exploitation to prove real-world impact
A vulnerability scan — it proves exploitability
A policy review
A backup test
scenarios.why: Scans enumerate potential vulnerabilities broadly; pen tests exploit them to demonstrate actual impact under ROE. When the question is 'could an attacker really do it,' only controlled exploitation answers it.
scenarios.hint: What proves exploitability rather than possibility?

scenarios.title: Cheapest defect
scenarios.situation: A CISO wants security defects caught as cheaply as possible in the SDLC.
scenarios.prompt: Where should the most effort go?
choices: Design and code phases — defects caught early cost orders of magnitude less than in production
Production monitoring only
Post-release pen testing only
User acceptance testing
scenarios.why: The cost of fixing a defect rises steeply the later it is found: design flaws fixed in design are cheap; the same flaw exploited in production costs incident response, downtime, and reputation. Shift-left via threat modeling and code review.
scenarios.hint: When is an architecture flaw cheapest to fix?

scenarios.title: Grading your own homework
scenarios.situation: The team that built the access-control system proposes to audit its effectiveness themselves.
scenarios.prompt: What is the problem, and what is the fix?
choices: Lack of independence — audits need organizational independence and objectivity to be credible
Audits are unnecessary
Only external auditors are ever valid
Self-audits are the gold standard

scenarios.title: Contain first
scenarios.situation: The SOC confirms malware beaconing from a workstation to an external server. The analyst's instinct is to immediately wipe and rebuild it.
scenarios.prompt: What does the NIST 800-61 incident response process prescribe first?
choices: Containment — isolate the host to stop spread and C2, before eradication and recovery
Eradication — wipe it now
Post-incident activity — write the report first
Preparation — buy new tools

scenarios.title: What to capture first
scenarios.situation: A suspected compromised server is still running. You get one shot at evidence collection before it is powered down.
scenarios.prompt: What do you capture first, and why?
choices: Memory (RAM) — it follows the order of volatility: registers/cache, RAM, then disk
The full disk image first
The system logs last week
The backup tapes
scenarios.why: The order of volatility (RFC 3227) dictates collection: most ephemeral first. RAM holds running processes, network connections, and encryption keys that vanish at power-off; disk images come after volatile data is preserved.
scenarios.hint: What disappears the moment power dies?

scenarios.title: Two plans, two purposes
scenarios.situation: A flood warning threatens the primary site. Executives ask which plan covers relocating staff to keep serving customers, versus restoring the servers.

choices: BCP keeps the business operating (people, processes, alternate sites); DRP restores IT systems and data
They are the same plan
BCP restores servers; DRP relocates staff
Neither covers floods
scenarios.why: Business continuity is about the business functioning through disruption — alternate sites, manual procedures, communications. Disaster recovery is the IT subset: restoring systems and data to meet RTO/RPO. DRP supports BCP; it does not replace it.
scenarios.hint: Which plan is about the business rather than the servers?

scenarios.title: Backing up to the RPO
scenarios.situation: A business impact analysis sets a 4-hour RPO for the order database.
scenarios.prompt: What does that require of backups?

One backup per week
Backups every 4 hours is overkill; daily is fine
RPO only applies to recovery time
scenarios.why: RPO answers 'how much data can we afford to lose,' measured in time: a 4-hour RPO means the freshest restorable backup can be no older than 4 hours. (RTO is the companion metric: how fast systems must be back.)

scenarios.title: Scoping the Capstone
scenarios.situation: You want to build a comprehensive security architecture for a mid-size enterprise for your portfolio. You have 4 weeks of evenings. You're tempted to add every feature you've learned.
scenarios.prompt: How do you scope the capstone for successful completion?

Build the most technically impressive version — complexity demonstrates advanced skills
Skip planning and start building — you'll figure out scope as you go
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A finished MVP proves competence; an unfinished ambitious project proves nothing. Employers value completed work with clear decisions. scenarios.title: When You're Stuck

scenarios.prompt: What's the most productive approach?

Keep pushing until it works — giving up on a technical challenge shows weakness
Abandon the current approach and rewrite everything using a different technology
Skip that feature entirely and pretend it was never planned
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Professional engineers timebox investigations and pivot strategically. Documenting the blocker and implementing a workaround shows problem-solving maturity. Endless grinding wastes capstone time. Rewriting introduces new risks. Pretending the feature was never planned is dishonest and loses a learning opportunity.
scenarios.hint: How do professional engineers handle blockers under deadline? What demonstrates maturity?

scenarios.title: Pre-Submission Review
scenarios.situation: Your comprehensive security architecture for a mid-size enterprise is functionally complete. You have 3 days before you want to publish it to your portfolio.
scenarios.prompt: What's the highest-value use of the remaining time?
choices: Polish and verify: test the demo end-to-end, proofread documentation, verify the README renders correctly, record a backup demo video, and do a final security/best-practices review
Add 2-3 more features to make it more impressive
Rewrite the code to be more elegant — first drafts are always messy
Publish immediately — done is better than perfect
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A polished, working project with great documentation beats a feature-rich buggy one. Demo failures during interviews are catastrophic. README quality signals professionalism. A backup video saves you if live demo fails. Adding features now risks breaking working code. Publishing without review risks embarrassing errors.
scenarios.hint: What causes the most damage in a portfolio review: missing features or broken demos?
evidence: Demo works | README complete | Video recorded | Security reviewed

scenarios.title: Defending Your Capstone
scenarios.situation: In a CISSP interview, the interviewer points to your comprehensive security architecture for a mid-size enterprise and asks: 'Walk me through your architecture. Why did you choose this approach over alternatives?'

List the technologies used — the stack speaks for itself
Explain that you followed best practices from your bootcamp
Focus on the code — offer to walk through the implementation line by line
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Interviewers assess judgment, not just knowledge. Narrating decisions with trade-offs shows engineering maturity. Listing technologies doesn't explain thinking. 'Best practices' without specifics sounds hollow. Line-by-line code walkthrough misses the architectural perspective they want.

lessons.title: CISSP — Security Architecture & Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: Access control models encode policy: DAC lets owners decide, MAC lets labels and clearances decide (government classifications), RBAC lets roles decide (enterprises). Non-discretionary models like MAC and RBAC remove per-user discretion.

Cryptography in three flavors: symmetric (one shared key, fast, bulk data — AES), asymmetric (key pairs, slow, key exchange and signatures — RSA, ECC), hashing (one-way integrity — SHA-256). Real systems are hybrid: asymmetric exchanges the symmetric key.

Security engineering layers defenses: defense in depth (overlapping controls), least privilege, fail-secure defaults, complete mediation (check every access), and economy of mechanism (keep it simple enough to verify).
Bell-LaPadula protects confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Biba protects integrity: no read down, no write up. Know which property each model guards — they are mirror images.
Business continuity starts with the BIA: identify critical processes, quantify RTO/RPO and impacts first. Recovery strategies and plans derive from the BIA, never the reverse.

Key management is the hard part of crypto: generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and destruction. The strongest cipher fails if keys are mishandled — and passwords need slow salted hashes, not encryption.

example.code:
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -in secrets.txt -out secrets.enc
openssl dgst -sha256 secrets.txt
example.walkthrough: The first command encrypts with AES-256-CBC — symmetric, fast bulk encryption, with a salt strengthening the password-derived key. The second hashes the original with SHA-256, giving you an integrity value you can verify later.

pitfalls: Common trap: encrypting passwords instead of hashing them — passwords need salted, slow hashes (bcrypt/Argon2), not reversible encryption.
Common trap: mixing up Bell-LaPadula and Biba — LaPadula guards confidentiality (no read up, no write down); Biba guards integrity.
Common trap: writing the DR plan before the BIA — recovery targets must come from business impact analysis first.
Common trap: trusting encryption alone — without key management and access controls, ciphertext is just obfuscation.

labs.title: Encrypt and Hash with OpenSSL
labs.objective: Practice symmetric encryption and integrity hashing with OpenSSL in the simulated terminal.
steps: Create a small plaintext file with echo 'sensitive data' > secrets.txt.
Encrypt it with openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -in secrets.txt -out secrets.enc.
Hash the original with openssl dgst -sha256 secrets.txt and record the digest.
Decrypt with openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -in secrets.enc and confirm it matches the original.

checks.hint: Run: openssl dgst -sha256 secrets.txt

labs.title: Password Hashing Done Right
labs.objective: Compare proper password hashing against naive approaches using OpenSSL's password hashing.
steps: Generate a SHA-512 crypt hash with openssl passwd -5 -salt abc123 'MyPassword'.
Generate it again with a different salt and observe that the output changes.
Note the $5$ prefix identifying the algorithm, and the salt embedded in the output.
Explain in one sentence why the salt defeats precomputed rainbow tables.

checks.hint: Run: openssl passwd -5 -salt abc123 'MyPassword'

simulations.title: What broke the report?
simulations.brief: The /api/report endpoint timed out at 09:20. The app log is the only witness. Read it like an investigator.

steps.symptom: GET /api/report returned 504 at 09:15 and timed out at 09:20.
evidence:
2026-10-04 09:14:47 ERROR connection refused: cache:6379
2026-10-04 09:14:48 WARN  retry 1/3 in 2s
2026-10-04 09:14:51 INFO  cache reachable, pool=10
2026-10-04 09:20:02 ERROR timeout after 30s: /api/report
options: The cache outage at 09:14 is the root cause — the report depends on it
The cache recovered at 09:14:51, so the 09:20 timeout is a separate issue — investigate the report query itself
Restart the cache — it is clearly unstable
The 504 and the timeout are unrelated coincidences
steps.explain: The log shows the cache recovered at 09:14:51 — five minutes before the 09:20 timeout. Correlating by time, not by narrative, separates the two incidents. The report query itself is now the suspect.

simulations.debrief: You correlated by timestamp instead of by story: the cache recovered before the timeout, so the report path gets its own investigation. Time is the investigator's first filter.

simulations.title: Contain or observe?
simulations.brief: The SOC sees anomalous outbound traffic from the app server. The CISO asks: contain now or observe to learn more?

steps.text: Anomalous outbound connections from the app server, pattern matches data staging. Call?

choices.label: Contain immediately — isolate the host
choices.feedback: Correct — suspected exfiltration in progress outranks intelligence gathering.

choices.label: Observe for 24h to map the attacker's full toolkit
choices.feedback: Observing active exfiltration to 'learn more' trades real data loss for hypothetical intel.

steps.text: Overnight the staging completed and 2GB left the network. Reconsider:

choices.label: Contain immediately
choices.feedback: Right — the cost of waiting just became measurable in gigabytes.

steps.text: Host isolated. Forensics wants the disk; legal wants the logs preserved first. Order?

choices.label: Image the disk first, then pull logs — disk is volatile
choices.feedback: Logs are the more volatile evidence here and the legal hold names them explicitly.

choices.label: Preserve logs first per the hold, then image the disk
choices.feedback: Correct — legal holds dictate evidence order; logs first, then the disk image.

simulations.debrief: You made the hard IR calls: contain active exfiltration immediately, and let the legal hold order the evidence collection.

simulations.title: Order the recovery
simulations.brief: The business continuity plan activates. Order the recovery so the business — not just IT — comes back first.

steps.context: BCP activation: declare, recover, resume, review.
items: Recover IT systems per the DRP
Declare the disaster and activate the plan
Resume business operations at the alternate site
Conduct the post-incident review

simulations.debrief: You ordered recovery around the business: declare, recover systems, resume operations, then review. IT recovery serves business resumption, not the reverse.

simulations.title: Harden the SSH config
simulations.brief: Review this sshd_config before the server goes live. Click the lines a CISSP would flag.

steps.config:
sshd_config:
1. Port 22
2. PermitRootLogin yes
3. PasswordAuthentication yes
4. MaxAuthTries 3
5. PermitEmptyPasswords no
6. X11Forwarding yes

issues.description: PermitRootLogin yes lets attackers target the highest-privilege account directly.
issues.fix: Set PermitRootLogin no (or prohibit-password) and require sudo from named accounts.

issues.description: PasswordAuthentication yes enables brute-force and credential-stuffing against SSH.
issues.fix: Set PasswordAuthentication no and require key-based authentication.

simulations.debrief: You flagged the SSH hardening classics: no root login, no password auth. Keys plus sudo is the baseline every hardening guide agrees on.

consoleSims.title: Triage the intrusion ticket
consoleSims.brief: Ticket INC-3091 reports anomalous outbound traffic. Triage it: prioritize, assign, and set the SLA clock.

tasks.instruction: Set INC-3091 priority to P1 — suspected exfiltration.
tasks.hint: Open the ticket and raise its priority to P1.

tasks.instruction: Assign INC-3091 to the SOC Tier-2 queue.
tasks.hint: Use the assignment control to route it to Tier-2.

consoleSims.debrief: You triaged the intrusion ticket by the book: P1 priority, Tier-2 ownership. Severity drives the response clock.

consoleSims.title: Write the detection rule
consoleSims.brief: Turn the log pattern into detection: alert on ERROR bursts in app.log going forward.

tasks.instruction: Create a detection rule named app-error-burst watching for ERROR in app.log.
tasks.hint: Create the rule with the ERROR pattern on the app.log source.

tasks.instruction: Set the rule threshold to 5 errors in 10 minutes, severity High.
tasks.hint: Configure the threshold and severity on the new rule.

consoleSims.debrief: You converted a manual grep into standing detection: pattern, threshold, severity. That is how assessments become controls.

sections.heading: Asset Security
items: Data classification — end-of-life media with restricted data needs sanitization matched to classification — destruction or crypto-erase — with certificates for audit. Ownership follows business accountability: the data owner decides classification based on value and sensitivity,…
Handling requirements — classification matches handling to harm: SSNs enable identity theft, so they get the highest tier with encryption, least-privilege access, and retention limits.
Data lifecycle — a legal hold overrides retention schedules: destroying potentially relevant data after notice is spoliation, with severe penalties.
Common trap — the security team classifies everything alone.
Common trap — delete faster before the hold is formalized.
Common trap — sell the servers as-is to recover value.
Common trap — keep everything forever to be safe.

sections.heading: Security Architecture
items: Security models — bell-LaPadula is the confidentiality model: the simple security property ('no read up') stops information flowing to lower clearances, and the *-property ('no write down') stops leaks downward.
Bell-LaPadula — biba is the classic integrity counterpart to Bell-LaPadula: it prevents low-integrity subjects from writing to high-integrity objects.
Biba — (Clark-Wilson also addresses integrity via transactions, but Biba is the canonical lattice integrity model.).
Symmetric ciphers like AES — are orders of magnitude faster for bulk data; asymmetric crypto (RSA, ECC) is used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk encryption.
Key management — revoke, rotate, audit for misuse, and enforce vault-based secret management with pre-commit scanning.
Common trap — useful, but the question asks for the classic integrity model.
Common trap — hashing the archive instead of encrypting.
Common trap — delete the commit and assume safety.
Common trap — change the repo to private and move on.

sections.heading: Network Security
items: Network segmentation — flat networks let any compromise reach everything; segmentation breaks the network into zones so a breach is contained and east-west traffic is filtered. IPsec operates at the network layer and is the standard for gateway-to-gateway site connectivity, encry…
DMZ — a DMZ (screened subnet) hosts public services between two firewall boundaries: the outer firewall filters internet traffic, the inner firewall strictly limits DMZ-to-internal flows.
VPNs — TLS VPNs suit remote users; PPTP is cryptographically broken and must not be used.
IDS vs IPS — an IDS only detects and alerts; an IPS sits inline and can drop malicious packets — at the cost that false positives become self-inflicted outages.
Detection controls — host controls matter, but architecture determines blast radius.
Common trap — directly on the internal LAN for easy management.
Common trap — a TLS/SSL VPN client on every desktop.

sections.heading: IAM
items: MFA — not all MFA is equal: SMS is vulnerable to SIM-swapping and interception, app codes resist that but remain phishable, while FIDO2 hardware keys bind authentication to the legitimate origin — the phishing-resistant choice.
Federation — SAML is the long-standing enterprise standard for browser-based SSO federation: the IdP authenticates once and asserts identity to each SaaS app.
SAML — kerberos suits on-prem Windows domains; OAuth/OIDC authorize and authenticate modern apps but SAML dominates enterprise SaaS federation.
Deprovisioning — joiner-mover-leaver processes must revoke access on termination automatically; manual, ticket-driven deprovisioning always lags.
Common trap — MFA is unnecessary with long passwords.
Common trap — authenticator apps are weaker than SMS.
Common trap — users need permanent accounts.

Shift-left — Shift-left via threat modeling and code review.
Independence — audit credibility rests on independence and objectivity: self-review invites blind spots and bias.
Common trap — only external auditors are ever valid.

Order of volatility — the order of volatility (RFC 3227) dictates collection: most ephemeral first.
